items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: But he became a close friend of Alban Berg so I remember Berg, who died when I was just six years old. But I remember him well because he was a close friend, and sometimes my father and he would take me to — well they were soccer fans and would go to soccer games.

ctx.x: Can you recall, as an 8-year-old, understanding why you had to leave the country?

Oh yes. I understood that. I mean I didn’t understand it on a very highly sophisticated level, but I absolutely knew — we still didn’t know at that time — that was before the Holocaust really, it was before — 1942 was really when that really evil stuff — but it was bad enough as it was. I remember even before, when I was about six or so, one of my aunts had a boyfriend who was — this was at my grandmother’s place — and like © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

everybody of a certain age there, he was forced into doing stuff for the government. And he was actually in a kind of labor gang, not full time, but they were working on building the famous Autobahn. And he had to wear a kind of uniform thing with a swastika armband. And I remember him arriving at my grandmother’s and tearing off this thing and throwing it in a corner and saying, you know, as if it was something dirty. He left very soon after. items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Alban Berg – who was a very close friend of my father’s and whom I saw a lot also – was one of the few people in Vienna among my father’s circle who had a car.

ctx.x: Why don’t you tell us about your ancestry, as much as you remember – your parents and even further back if you . . .

It’s a fairly complicated – but I’ll try to be brief. My father was born in what was then the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Between the world wars it was Poland. After World War II it became the Soviet Union, but now it’s Ukraine. So it had a scattered history. He was born into a Hassidic family, but not in what we generally think of as eastern European Jewry. We mostly think of what they call a stetl, which is a small

town or a village. This was not even a village. It was just a collection of farmhouses, a very small spot on the map. My paternal grandfather was the manager of an estate that belonged to a Polish noblewoman. So my father grew up in a rural atmosphere. Like most Jewish kids, he went to – very early on to a school where you learn to read Hebrew. So he grew up multi­ lingual: Polish, Russian, Ukrainian.
